list.listitem: Ultrasound with cyst morphology and Doppler flow studies are helpful to distinguish benign cysts from ovarian malignancies. B
Oral contraceptives are not helpful for the treatment of ovarian cysts. They can prevent functional cysts in premenopausal women. B
Most simple ovarian cysts will resolve within 3 months without treatment. B

background.definition: An ovarian cyst is a sac filled with fluid or a semi-solid material that develops on or near an ovary. A simple cyst has no septations, solid areas, or papillary projections.

list.listitem: Three percent to 18% of women, depending on the frequency of ultrasound.
A study of transvaginal ultrasound in premenopausal women showed a prevalence of 6.6%.

In another study, benign ovarian lesions were found in approximately 4% of 644 asymptomatic Swedish women aged 20 to 39 years with no history of gynecological disease. Lesions included endometriomas in ten and dermoid cyst in five. Among cysts that were surgically removed in one study, 58% were dermoid cysts.
In the University of Kentucky Ovarian Cancer Screening Trial which enrolled 47,762 individuals over 30 years, 5.5% had incident ovarian cysts.
An autopsy study reported a prevalence of 15.4% in postmenopausal women. In another study, the frequency of simple cysts in postmenopausal women was 17% to 24%.

In a case series of 171 verified cases of non-traumatic hemoperitoneum identified in a single emergency department, 76% of cases were in women and the most common cause was ruptured ovarian cyst (n=76).

Benign ovarian tumors are associated with an increased risk of ovarian cancer based on a meta-analysis of 10 primarily case-control studies including 10,331 patients with ovarian malignancy (RR 1.4, 95% CI 1.01 - 1.9). There was high study heterogeneity.
Can be functional, benign, or malignant.
Functional cysts include follicular and corpus luteum cysts. Most fetal ovarian cysts are thought to be caused by excessive stimulation of the fetal ovaries by placental and maternal hormones.
Benign cysts include endometriomas, dermoid cysts (teratomas), and serous or mucous cystadenomas.

Other benign non-functional cysts or cyst-like masses include hydrosalpinges, peritoneal inclusion cysts (can be located adjacent to or surrounding a functioning ovary), mesenteric cyst of Mullerian origin, and Tarlov cysts (deep cystic masses communicating with sacral foramina).

Ovarian cyst development is a common adverse event during immunosuppression treatment with mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR) inhibitors (sirolimus, everolimus, and temsirolimus), occurring in 37% (95% CI 16% to 58%) based on a meta-analysis of 7 studies including 406 women. The pooled incidence of clinically significant ovarian cysts was 17.3% (95% CI 5.6-29.1%).
Malignant cysts include borderline tumors (low malignant potential) and ovarian cystadenocarcinoma.
Functional cysts and corpus luteum cysts form as part of the normal physiologic process of ovulation.
Small follicles develop early in the menstrual cycle, and one becomes a dominant follicle.

After the follicle ruptures and the oocyte is released, a corpus luteum cyst forms. The corpus luteum cyst will usually regress in the absence of fertilization, but in a pregnant woman, the cyst will first increase and then gradually decrease in size.
Endometriomas are blood-filled cysts in patients with endometriosis caused by ectopic endometrial tissue in the ovaries.
Ovarian neoplasms are caused by abnormal overgrowth of cells in the ovary, either benign or malignant.
Transabdominal and/or transvaginal ultrasound is the test of choice for diagnosis and evaluation of ovarian cysts. B
Ultrasound with cyst morphology and Doppler flow studies are helpful to distinguish benign cysts from ovarian malignancies. B

Differential.Differential_Features: Hyperandrogenism and menstrual irregularities in addition to multiple cysts
Elevated CA-125, complex cyst, systemic symptoms
Sexually transmitted infection risk factors, pelvic pain, cervical motion tenderness
Positive pregnancy test, adnexal pain, hemodynamic instability

list.listitem: Patients may present with pelvic fullness/pressure (large cysts); sharp, sudden pain (ruptured ovarian cyst); intermittent pain (ovarian torsion); or cyclic pain (endometriosis).
Symptoms and signs suggestive of malignancy include persistent pelvic/abdominal pain, urinary urgency/frequency, increased abdominal size/bloating, and difficulty eating.
Pelvic examination has limited sensitivity for detection of adnexal mass, especially as body mass index increases.
Pelvic examination is also not reliable at distinguishing malignant from nonmalignant cause.

Infection of ovarian cysts appears to be uncommon. A report of 12 cases over 14 years at a single institution appeared in 1966 with most patients presenting with abdominal pain; all but 1 patient were febrile at the time of admission. Authors of a case series of 50 Japanese patients diagnosed with ovarian cyst infection noted that only 3 cases were diagnosed accurately prior to surgery; most were accidental findings with 16 discovered during a physical exam and 24 discovered during surgeries for other lesions.

In an industry-sponsored trial to develop a testing algorithm using genes and serum biomarkers to predict malignancy of female pelvic masses, investigators found a combination of 8 genes and 4 biomarkers had an area under the curve of 95.1% (95% CI 92.0% to 98.2%) using a group of 183 patients with known histologic diagnoses, including 57% with benign disease. The algorithm identified 98.9% of patients with stage III-IV epithelial ovarian cancer.

Ultrasound is the imaging modality of choice. Ultrasound with Doppler flow and cyst morphology can increase specificity and is recommended for postmenopausal women. Doppler flow adds a significant contribution by differentiating a true solid component from a solid-appearing component or debris within a cyst.

The American College of Radiology (ACR) recommends ultrasound (US) duplex Doppler pelvic, US pelvis transabdominal, and/or US pelvis transvaginal as usually appropriate for initial imaging of pre- or postmenopausal women with a clinically suspected adnexal mass and no acute symptoms.

The 2020 Canadian guidelines on "Initial Investigation and Management of Benign Ovarian Masses" notes that simple, unilocular and hemorrhagic cysts; endometriomas; mature cystic teratomas (dermoid); and fibromas typically demonstrate classic benign features on ultrasound.

Despite the high specificity of ultrasound for adnexal masses, false negatives do occur. In one series of 318 women with adnexal masses who underwent histopathological evaluation, three premenopausal women had more serious disease including large endometrioid ovarian adenocarcinoma, a bilocular cyst diagnosed as borderline mucinous tumor, and a unilocular-solid cyst diagnosed as borderline serous tumor.
Real-time sonoelastography may be a useful adjunct for distinguishing benign vs. malignant ovarian lesions, the former has softer tissue properties.

MRI: accuracy is similar to ultrasound, and generally does not add to the diagnosis. Although the positive likelihood ratio (LR) is not high (6), MRI has a fairly high sensitivity for ruling out malignancy (negative LR 0.09).

The ACR recommends MRI with intravenous (IV) contrast when an adnexal mass is indeterminate on ultrasound, either because it is unclear whether the mass is benign or malignant or the organ of origin is uncertain.

In a prospective, multicenter non-inferiority study that included 133 18-40-year-old non-pregnant women with non-traumatic acute/subacute abdominal pain, MRI demonstrated non-inferiority diagnostic accuracy compared to CT. The most common diagnoses were non-specific pain (30.1%), ovarian cyst rupture (12.8%), and appendicitis (9.7%). A strategy of MRI followed by CT when the MRI was normal had a diagnostic accuracy of 91%.
In cases of suspected adnexal torsion, susceptibility-weighted MR sequence can be helpful.

Authors of a systematic review of 59 studies on the application of AI to ultrasound imaging in the diagnosis and management of benign gynecological disorders found that most studies were attempting to distinguishing between normal and pathological causes and the rest (n=19) to automatically segment or measure aspects of the findings such as ovarian volume or endometrial thickness. The authors found high risk of bias for the subject selection and lack of external validation.
Cyst aspiration has poor sensitivity and risks seeding malignant cells.

Ovarian cysts are sometimes aspirated intraoperatively and occasionally for diagnostic purposes. In one case series of 459 ovarian cysts with fine needle aspiration (FNA) specimens, cyst fluid cytology had 100% specificity and 54% sensitivity for the detecting ovarian malignancies. Most cysts (90.6%) were benign, 7.0% were diagnosed as atypical, 0.9% as suspicious, and 1.5% as malignant. Of 300 specimens with corresponding surgical pathology, the rate of malignancy for benign FNA, including borderline neoplasms, was 10 of 264 specimens (3.8%), for atypical FNA was 0%, and for suspicious or malignant FNA was 12 of 12 specimens (100%).
Laparoscopy with cystectomy or oophorectomy is definitive for diagnosis.
CT is less specific than MRI or ultrasound. PET scan and CA-125 are not reliable.

The IOTA group's Simple Rules can be applied to predict malignancy risk; sensitivity and specificity are 0.93; 95% CI 0.89–0.95 and 0.81; 95% CI 0.76–0.85, respectively. IOTA Simple Rules include 10 features; 5, called B features, are used to predict a benign adnexal mass and the other 5, called M features, are used to predict a malignant mass. B features include unilocular cyst, solid components present but that are <7 mm, acoustic shadows, smooth multilocular tumor, largest diameter <100 mm, and no blood flow. M features include irregular solid tumor, ascites, at least 4 papillary structures, irregular multilocular-solid tumor, largest diameter 100 mm, and very strong flow.

Although most ovarian cysts are found incidentally on ultrasound or bimanual examination done for other reasons, patients may present with pelvic fullness/pressure from large cysts; sharp, sudden pain from a ruptured cyst; intermittent pain from ovarian torsion; or cyclic pain from endometriosis.
Premenopausal woman: obtain pregnancy test, ultrasound with Doppler flow/morphology.

Postmenopausal woman: obtain CA-125 level, ultrasound with Doppler flow/morphology. ACR notes that CA-125 levels improved specificity of diagnosing a malignant ovarian tumor only in lesions already suspected to be malignant on US.
Oral contraceptives (OCs) are not helpful for the treatment of ovarian cysts. A
Cyst aspiration is not recommended for diagnosis or treatment. B
Laparoscopic surgery is recommended for persistent or suspicious cysts; surgery is unnecessary in most patients with simple cysts. C

Although OCs can prevent the development of ovarian cysts, they are not useful for treatment. Most cysts resolve within a few cycles without treatment. If a cyst persists, further work-up is suggested as the cyst may be pathological (eg, endometrioma or para-ovarian cyst) not physiological.

Authors of a Cochrane review found no evidence to support use of adjuvant therapy for borderline ovarian tumors. In addition, in one trial, bilateral cystectomy versus cystectomy and contralateral oophorectomy for women with bilateral borderline ovarian tumors resulted in a significantly increased chance of pregnancy without a significantly increased risk of recurrence.
Cysts can be removed at laparoscopy; however, this is unnecessary in most patients with simple cysts.

If surgery is needed for a symptomatic ovarian mass characterized as benign on ultrasound, the Canadian 2020 guidelines recommend consideration of unilateral or bilateral oophorectomy for postmenopausal women and ovarian cystectomy for premenopausal women, if technically feasible. In addition, they recommend peritoneal washing for cytology and frozen section for analysis at the time of surgical management of an ovarian mass if there is a suspicion of malignancy.
Consider surgical referral for cysts larger than 10 cm, complex cysts, and women with elevated CA-125 levels.

A laparoscopic approach is appropriate even with large (>10 cm) masses; however, laparoscopic ovarian cystectomy is associated with a reduction in ovarian reserve (possibly due to damage to ovarian vessels) compared to removal at laparotomy.

In one observational study of 80 women with benign ovarian cyst undergoing cyst removal, use of transvaginal laparoendoscopic single-site surgery in 40 of them compared to transumbilical laparoendoscopic single-site surgery was similar with respect to operation time, intra-operative blood loss, and hospitalization costs. It was, however, associated with significantly faster time to ambulation and return of bowel function with less postoperative pain level and shorter hospital length of stay.

In a feasibility study comparing transvaginal natural orifice translumenal endoscopic surgery to conventional laparoscopy for ovarian cystectomy (58 patients in each group), investigators found the groups comparable in ability to follow recommended surgical technique without deviation to alternative surgical methods. This surgical approach has been used for gynecologic, gastroenterological and urologic conditions primarily in other countries and the literature on this technique is scarce.

Intraoperative rupture of benign ovarian cysts is associated with increased risk for benign recurrence (RR 3.1, 95% CI 1.05-9.1) but not with adverse short- or long-term outcomes including reoperation or infertility based on a systematic review and meta-analysis of 28 studies. One author recommended use of Maryland forceps with gentle open and close dissecting motions only and avoidance of grasping the cyst wall to allow correct identification of the cleavage plane for dissection and avoid cyst rupture.

In one study of 52 women undergoing ovarian cyst removal, investigators found that cyst size was predictive of subsequent reduction in ovarian reserve with only larger ovarian cysts of 5 cm or more showing a statistically significant reduction in anti-Müllerian hormone postoperatively.

In an Italian study of 13 postmenarchal girls with hemorrhagic corpus luteum cysts requiring intervention, 11 presented with persistent abdominal pain. Ultrasound examination showed complex ovarian masses in 77% cases and simple ovarian masses in the rest. Laparoscopic excision was performed in more than 45% cases but laparotomy was commonly required. At 2 years follow-up, there were no recurrences and regular menses were reported.

Authors of a systematic review found that use of electrodiathermy during ovarian cystectomy was accompanied by increased damage to ovarian reserve compared to ovarian sutures. The Canadian 2020 guidelines state that electrocautery for hemostasis should be used sparingly in order to reduce the risk of damage to healthy ovarian tissue and minimize adhesion formation.
The majority of simple cysts will resolve without treatment.
The Canadian 2020 guidelines recommend laparoscopic ovarian cystectomy over fenestration and aspiration for removal of cystic masses.

Cyst aspiration does not appear to improve the rate of resolution compared with expectant management, although trial data are limited. In one older RCT of 269/278 women available for 6-month follow-up, there were no differences in rate of cyst resolution between aspiration and expectant management (46% [59/128] vs. 44.6% [63/141], respectively).

In one long-term follow-up study of 24 women with persistent ovarian cysts undergoing transvaginal aspiration, recurrence rate was 75%. A more recent study reported a recurrence rate of 20.2% (17/84) undergoing aspiration for simple ovarian cysts <80 mm.

Authors of a systematic review and meta-analysis of 8 studies of recurrent endometriomas found that recurrence rates following a single aspiration ranged from 28.9% to 91.5%. The addition of sclerotherapy did not appear to improve recurrence rates. However, repeated aspiration can reduce the recurrence rate to 5.4% by the sixth aspiration.
The majority of simple cysts will resolve without treatment within 3 months. B

In the University of Kentucky Ovarian Cancer Screening Trial including 2,638 individuals with incident cysts, 62% experienced resolution within 1.2 years. Time to resolution was shorter for unilocular vs. septated cysts (mean 1.9 years vs 2.6 years, respectively) and for smaller vs. larger cysts. A faster cyst resolution rate also occurred in those older than age 70 years and not using hormone therapy.
Functional cysts can cause problems if they rupture or lead to ovarian torsion, but this is rare. C

Among 41/66 adolescent and pediatric patients treated with ovarian cystectomy for dermoid cysts who received follow-up, seven (17%) had recurrent or persistent dermoid cysts; two required repeat surgery. Type of surgery did not influence dermoid recurrence.

Data regarding oncogenic potential of ovarian cysts are limited. Authors of a meta-analysis of 34 studies found malignancy rates of 1.1% (95% CI 0.74-1.66), including borderline malignancy in 0.6%, for the 2177 surgically-removed unilocular ovarian cysts and 0.9% (95% CI 0.57-1.35), including 0.3% with borderline malignancy, for the 2290 surgically-removed lesions classified on ultrasound as anechoic unilocular cysts. Malignancy rates were lower for premenopausal vs. postmenopausal women (0.6% vs. 3.2%, for unilocular cysts, and 0.3% vs. 1.9% for anechoic cysts, respectively).
Single or multiple inclusion cysts (anechoic ovarian cysts up to 10 mm in diameter) in postmenopausal women do not place women at increased cancer risk.B
Less than 0.1% of unilocular ovarian cysts with a diameter of less than 10 cm will be malignant. B
Serum anti-Mullerian hormone may be useful for following ovarian reserve following cystectomy. B

Women with ovarian masses that contain highly worrisome features or other signs of malignancy (e.g., symptomatic, large (>10 cm), associated with elevated CA 125 level) at follow-up should be referred for surgery.

The Canadian 2020 guidelines recommend that asymptomatic patients with ovarian masses characterized as benign on ultrasound be followed initially by repeat ultrasound in 8 to 12 weeks, preferably in the proliferative phase of the menstrual cycle for premenopausal women. Follow-up ultrasound can then be done yearly for masses that remain stable and do not develop malignant features.

Although the likelihood of malignancy in a stable ovarian cyst is small, the risk of continued monitoring includes incidental findings, an increased likelihood of unnecessary surgery, patient anxiety and cost.

If the surgical pathology results reveal malignancy in an ovarian mass, the Canadian 2020 guidelines recommend comprehensive surgical staging should be performed by a surgeon with expertise in gynecologic oncology, if resources permit.
The risk of ovarian malignancy increases with age.
In one screening ultrasound study of 515 Australian healthy postmenopausal women, both ovaries were visualized in 71% and ovarian/paraovarian abnormalities were seen in 12.6%.
One percent to 2% of pregnancies will be complicated by an ovarian cyst.
Low-level elevation of CA-125 is normal in pregnancy.
Ultrasound, transabdominal and transvaginal, is the imaging modality of choice (ACR). MRI without contrast can be used for further characterization following ultrasound if needed.
The risk of malignancy is 0.9% to 3%; most of these are low malignant potential tumors.

In a case series of 236 Korean pregnant women who underwent surgery for an ovarian mass, 223 (94.5%) had a benign mass and 13 women (5.5%) had a malignant mass. The Sassone scoring system, including features of inner wall structure, wall thickness, septum and echogenicity had an area under the ROC curve of 0.831 for determining malignancy.
Large cysts may lead to torsion or obstructed labor, but this is rare.

Cochrane authors found no RCTs investigating laparoscopic surgery for benign ovarian tumors during pregnancy. Case series suggest safety but potential risks include abnormally high serum levels of carbon dioxide from infusion of gas and perforation of internal organs which may also harm the fetus.

Authors of a systematic review and meta-analysis of surgery for pregnant women with adnexal masses found 11 studies comparing laparoscopy with laparotomy and 4 comparing elective vs emergent surgery. Laparoscopy was associated with shorter length of hospital stay but similar risk of spontaneous abortion and preterm delivery compared to laparotomy. Elective surgery was associated with a decreased risk of preterm delivery compared to emergent surgery (OR 0.13; 95% CI, 0.04-0.48).

In a single tertiary-care institution case series including 135 pregnant patients of whom 110 underwent elective and 25 underwent emergency surgery for benign ovarian cysts, the rates of laparoscopic surgery (98.2% vs. 52.0%) and ovarian conservation (99.1% vs. 80.0%) were significantly higher, with fewer post-surgical hospitalization days (4.6 ± 1.3 vs. 9.8 ± 10.5 days) in elective vs. emergency cases. There was no significant differences in gestational age at delivery, preterm birth rate or birth weight.

Based on three clinical trials, there is insufficient evidence to determine whether drainage of functional ovarian cysts prior to controlled ovarian hyperstimulation as treatment for subfertility influences clinical pregnancy rate; live birth rates were not reported.

Fetal ovarian cysts occur in an estimated 1 in 2600 pregnancies and about 1 in 2500 live births. Most are thought to be benign functional cysts due to an abnormal response to maternal gonadotropin and estrogen inducing follicular cyst growth and pseudo-maturation. The majority regress, but some fetuses and neonates experience ovarian torsion or intracystic hemorrhage. Ovarian malignancy is extremely rare with only one case reported in the literature. Optimal management is uncertain.

Fetal ovarian cysts are diagnosed by ultrasound and classified as simple or complex. MRI can be used in cases for which ultrasound is unsatisfactory or to confirm the presence of female genitalia and delineate gastrointestinal and genitourinary anatomy.

Consensus guidelines on minimally-invasive management of fetal ovarian cysts are offered by the Italian Society of Videosurgery in Infancy; details on management considerations are described in this paper. For simple cysts, they recommend weekly prenatal ultrasound monitoring if cyst diameter is <4 cm and consideration of prenatal cyst aspiration if larger, as these are associated with a higher risk of torsion. Postnatal ultrasound can be scheduled every 3-6 weeks until cyst regression. For complex cysts, they recommend prenatal ultrasound every 3-6 weeks with possible term delivery, and postnatal elective surgical excision using an open, video-assisted or laparoscopic technique.

The 2023 European Paediatric Surgeons' Association Consensus Statement on the Management of Neonatal Ovarian Simple Cysts found limited data on potential benefits and complications of prenatal ultrasound-guided aspiration. They recommend that neonates with simple ovarian cysts >4 cm be offered surgical interventions within 2 weeks of life. Their preferred approach is complete laparoscopic cyst aspiration and fenestration with bipolar instruments. Neonates managed with prenatal cyst aspiration should be followed for 6 months. Ultrasound follow-up after a conservative approach should occur every 3 to 4 months until 1 year.

Authors of a systematic review and meta-analysis of 34 studies with 954 fetuses found that about half (53.8% of the 784 cases followed) resolved during pregnancy or after birth. Resolution was significantly lower in cases with complex vs simple cysts (odds ratio [OR] 0.15; 95% CI 0.10-0.23) and with cysts measuring ≥40 mm (OR 0.03; 95% CI 0.01-0.06). Torsion occurred more often in those larger cysts (OR 30.8; 95% CI 8.6-110). In fetuses undergoing prenatal cyst aspiration, post-natal recurrence was 37.9% (95% CI, 14.8-64.3%). Post-natal ovarian torsion occurred in 10.8% and intracystic hemorrhage in 12.8%, and 21.8% (95% CI, 0.9-40.0%) had surgery.

In a retrospective cohort study of 102 fetuses with ovarian cyst, 92 of which were simple cysts, spontaneous resolution was significantly higher among cases with simple vs. complex cysts (76.1% vs 20%) and for cysts <4 cm than cysts ≥4 cm (50/56 or 89.3% vs 22/46 or 47.8%). Ovarian torsion was confirmed in 4.9%, but prenatal cyst characteristics and size did not predict torsion risk.

In a multicenter Canadian study of 189 female infants with congenital ovarian cysts, median gestational age at diagnosis was 33 weeks and median maximal prenatal cyst diameter was 40 mm. Cysts resolved spontaneously in 62%, 14 (7%) prenatally and the remainder at a median age of 124 days. Prenatal aspiration was conducted in 3%, ovary sparing resection in 23%, and oophorectomy in 74% with surgery occurring at a median age of 7.4 weeks. There was no significant difference in the odds of ovarian preservation (OR 3.06, 95% CI 0.86 -13.2) between the 22 patients who underwent early surgery compared to the 131 observed for at least 3 months.

In an open RCT of in-utero aspiration (IUA) of anechoic fetal ovarian cysts vs. expectant management in 61 fetuses, there was no significant difference in incidence of neonatal intervention between groups (20.6% vs. 37.0%, respectively; relative risk (RR) 0.55; 95% CI 0.24-1.27). Of the 34 cases randomized to IUA, 31/34 procedures were uneventful, 2 could not be performed due to fetal position and 1 resulted in a dry tap. Cyst resolution was significantly more frequent with IUA vs. expectant management (47.1% vs. 18.5%, respectively) and there was a reduced rate of oophorectomy (3.0% vs 22.0%), although this did not reach statistical significance.

In a case series of 752 children (mean age 13.7 years) at a single institution in Texas who underwent surgery over 10 years for adnexal masses, 93.7% were benign, 0.9% were borderline, and 5.4% were malignant. Only one malignant mass was cystic and the remainder were heterogeneous. Malignant masses were associated with elevated tumor markers, primarily alpha fetoprotein, beta human chorionic gonadotropin, cancer antigen 125, and lactate dehydrogenase. Of all 781 masses, 66.6% were ovarian and the remainder were paratubal or tubal.

In a retrospective study of 80 Swiss children with adnexal pathology, the presence of vomiting, short abdominal pain duration, and elevated CRP level were predictive of ovarian torsion vs. only ovarian cyst (the latter found in 63 cases).

In a 6-year retrospective study of 814 females aged 2-21 years who underwent surgery for an ovarian cyst or neoplasm at 10 children's hospitals, 22% had torsion. Younger age, mass size >5 cm, abdominal pain, and vomiting had an increased likelihood of torsion; torsion was not associated with increased risk of malignancy.

Based on data on 6028 children from a Nationwide Readmission Database who were admitted with ovarian torsion and underwent either total oophorectomy or ovarian preservation surgery, 41% had ovarian cyst and 0.4% had a malignant mass. The overall readmission rate was 4%, with no difference between surgical approaches. Readmission diagnoses were cyst (10%), malignant mass (9%), benign mass (7%), and torsion (5%).
